newsitem.title: USA: German banks see no halfway house for UK over EMU.
newsitem.headline: German banks see no halfway house for UK over EMU.

text.p: Germany's powerful banks would welcome Britain into European monetary union with open arms, but they are not prepared to sit back and watch the U.K. reap the benefits of the euro without bearing any obligations.

The chief executives and economists of Germany's largest commercial banks, gathered in Washington for international meetings, said British participation in the single currency would strengthen the euro by giving it a larger market base.
With Britain's ruling Conservative party deeply divided on its attitude to Europe, most bankers believed it was unlikely that sterling would be merged into the Euro from the start.

Even with political backing for the project, Britain may find itself not eligible to join EMU in the first round -- given that sterling has still not rejoined the European Exchange Rate Mechanism which it abandoned abruptly in 1992.

But the bankers, signalling that they at least could turn a blind eye to sterling's prolonged absence from the ERM, said it would be regrettable if London remained outside the euro area at the currency's inception and urged Britain to join.

"I am quite sure that EMU will start even without Britain," said Juergen Sarrazin, chief executive of Dresdner Bank. "And it can be, at least in the beginning, a success without Britain and other countries.
"But I would deeply regret it if Britain does not join. For me, the U.K. should be an integral part of it. ... I hope, and I think all Europeans do, that they will join us as soon as possible."
The euro's launch in 1999 is expected simultaneously to establish the world's largest one-currency debt market outside the United States and create a new major reserve currency.

Hilmar Kopper, chief executive of Germany's largest commercial bank, Deutsche Bank AG, said he believed this would put Britain under huge pressure to join the single currency within a few years of its launch.
"The Brits will not be in initially I think," he said. "But once it is up and running they will be in within three years. The City needs to be there."

Despite their words of encouragement for Europe's largest financial centre, the banks were adamant that Britain should not be given an open pass key to the planned TARGET payment system unless it took the plunge and joined the Euro.
The German banks, backed by the Bundesbank, have united in opposition to London's pleas that it be allowed to use the planned TARGET international payment system as a full member.
"We are strictly against privileges for London which are not accompanied by duties as a result of participation in monetary union," Albrecht Schmidt, chief executive at Bayerische Vereinsbank, said.
The Bank of England has argued vehemently that it must be given full access to TARGET regardless of whether or not it takes part in EMU from the outset.

This would allow it to create liquidity in euros by offering intraday and overnight credits in the currency, which the Germans and other continental Europeans argue could pose problems for the European Central Bank's monetary policy.
England's argument that any decision to deny it this right would be discriminatory has cut no ice with the fiercely inflation-conscious Bundesbank or conservative German banks.

"Nowhere else in the world is a central bank allowed to offer intra-day credits in a currency for which it bears no responsibility," said Karl-Heinz Wessel, president of the German banking association.
"Why should it be any different in this case? This is what we have to make clear to the British," he added.
But for Ulrich Ramm, chief economist at Commerzbank, the TARGET issue was just one aspect of a deeper-seated British attitude problem with respect to EMU.
Ramm said it was hard to shake the view that the City's attitude was increasingly being driven by pure self-interest.

"Yes, we would like Britain to be in, but as a European," he said. "I sometimes get the feeling in the City that the decision is being taken not on the basis of whether it is good for Europe or even good for Britain for it to be in or out, but on the basis of how the City can get most out of it."
